title: Raising meat birds for the table
subtitle: Running a small batch of fast-growing table birds from day-old to dispatch.
excerpt: Meat birds reach slaughter weight in seven to ten weeks from day-old, a far shorter cycle than keeping laying hens. The arc involves sourcing the right breed of chick, brooding through the first three weeks, moving to a grower pen with outdoor access, and dispatching cleanly at the end. A small batch of twenty birds is manageable for most smallholders with a basic setup.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Meat Chickens (2018). RSPCA Assured standards for meat chickens (2023). Lewis Wright, The Practical Poultry Keeper (1867), Internet Archive, chapters on table poultry. Gail Damerow, Storey's Guide to Raising Chickens (2017), chapter on meat birds.

glossaryTerms.definition: A chicken bred and raised for the quality of its meat rather than for egg production. Table breeds are typically broad-chested, with a high feed-conversion ratio.

The air temperature needed under or near a heat source for newly hatched chicks, starting at around 35 degrees at ground level in the first week and reduced by around 3 degrees per week until chicks are fully feathered.

A chick that has hatched within the last 24 to 48 hours and has not yet begun eating or drinking. Day-old chicks absorb the yolk sac before hatching and can travel safely for up to 48 hours without food or water.

projectSchedule.title: Chicks arrive
projectSchedule.body: Day-old chicks arrive or hatch. Brooder running at correct temperature. Fresh water and starter crumb immediately available.

projectSchedule.title: First week check
projectSchedule.body: Check weight gain, droppings, behaviour. Reduce brooding temperature by 3 degrees. Clean and refill feeders and drinkers daily.

projectSchedule.title: Move to grower pen
projectSchedule.body: Chicks fully feathered enough for outdoor access in good weather. Move to larger grower pen. Switch from starter to grower ration.

projectSchedule.title: Assess growth
projectSchedule.body: Fast-growing commercial cross breeds may be approaching dispatch weight. Heritage and slow-growing breeds need another two to four weeks. Weigh a sample of birds.

projectSchedule.title: Dispatch window begins
projectSchedule.body: Commercial cross breeds typically reach 2.5 to 3 kg liveweight. Heritage breeds at 10 to 16 weeks depending on breed and target size. Dispatch cleanly and process promptly.

content.text: A batch of
table birds
is a rewarding project. Chicks go from
day-old chick
to the table in eight to twelve weeks. The result is slow-grown poultry at a fraction of the shop price.
Choosing a breed

Fast-growing commercial crosses (Cobb 500-type, Ross 308, Hubbard JA57) reach dispatch weight in six to eight weeks. They need careful management to avoid leg problems from rapid growth. Heritage and slow-growing breeds (Dorking, Sussex, Ixworth, Label Rouge-type) take ten to sixteen weeks but are more robust outdoors and produce more flavour.
For a first batch, a slow-growing commercial cross or a recognised heritage breed is more forgiving than the fastest-growing types.
Setting up the brooder
Chicks need a warm area from the moment they arrive. The
brooding temperature
under a heat plate should be around 35 degrees at chick level in the first week. A heat plate (electric hen) is safer than a heat lamp and gives a more natural day-night temperature cycle.
Run the brooder for at least two hours before chicks arrive so the temperature is stable.
Allow at least 0.1 m squared of floor space per chick in the brooder. Overcrowded chicks compete for heat and feeder space and grow unevenly.
Lay a 5 cm layer of clean wood shavings across the floor. Paper towels over the top for the first two or three days help chicks find the feed.
Place water drinkers and crumb feeders within 30 cm of the heat source so chicks eat and drink immediately after warming.
Weeks one to three: brooder management
Check chicks within the first hour: all should be eating, drinking, and moving freely. Chicks piled under the heat source are cold; chicks pressed against the far walls are too hot.
Reduce the heat plate height (increasing air temperature gap) by around 3 degrees each week. By week three, most healthy chicks need no supplemental heat in a sheltered indoor environment.
Clean drinkers daily; refresh feeders twice daily. Chicks foul their water very quickly; dirty water is the most common source of early disease problems.
Add grit from the second week. Chicks eating whole grains or foraging on litter need insoluble grit to grind food in their gizzard.
Moving to the grower pen

At three to four weeks, fully feathered chicks can move to a larger pen with outdoor access in mild weather. Outdoor space of at least 2 m squared per bird is the welfare standard for free-range production. A simple arc or moveable pen keeps birds on fresh ground and distributes manure across the pasture.

Switch from starter crumb (high protein, around 22%) to a grower ration (around 18% protein) at the same time. Continuing high-protein starter into the finisher period pushes rapid growth that can stress the skeleton of faster-growing breeds.
Finishing and dispatch

Weigh a sample of birds at six weeks and assess their breast development by feel. The keel bone should be well covered with muscle and fat on a bird ready for dispatch. A prominent keel means the bird needs more time.

Dispatch on farm for home consumption is legal in England and Wales for chickens without a licence. Pluck and gut within an hour of dispatch while the carcass is still warm. Chill to below 4 degrees within two hours.

attrs.cue: Several birds sitting down and reluctant to move at five weeks
attrs.cause: Leg weakness from rapid growth in a fast-growing type; may also indicate coccidiosis in young birds
attrs.fix: Check droppings for blood (coccidiosis sign). Ensure drinkers are clean and floor space is adequate. Reduce feed for two days if birds are very heavy relative to their age: slowing growth temporarily can allow the skeleton to catch up.

attrs.cause: Overcrowding, insufficient feeder space, or bright light stressing birds
attrs.fix: Reduce light levels; ensure at least one feeder position per five birds. Move to outdoor access as soon as weather permits.
